The EU, the UK and many small nations rejected a pact that promoted carbon capture and omitted a commitment to move away from fossil fuels.

After 44 hours of overtime on top of two weeks of negotiations, COP31 ended on Sunday without a climate agreement.

The so-called Antalya Pact failed after several countries, including the EU, the UK and many small Pacific island states, rejected a final draft that made no mention of fossil fuels – the leading cause of climate change. 

In fact, the pact proposed by co-hosts Türkiye and Australia did not even refer to the “transition away from fossil fuels”, or TAFF, the landmark agreement reached at COP28 in Dubai.

For a global population facing stronger, more unpredictable weather and ecosystem collapse, the failure to agree on a fossil fuel phaseout or provide climate finance to developing nations means another year without a collective action plan in a rapidly warming world.

More than a decade after nearly 200 countries agreed to limiting global warming to 1.5°C at COP21 in Paris – also known as the Paris Agreement – 2026 is on course to become the second calendar year to exceed that threshold. The UN warns that a long-term breach will happen soon, too, with every fraction of a degree increasing the risk of irreversible environmental damage.

“There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres said after the summit.

But is there reason for hope anyway? While COP31’s failure marks a setback, some think the acrimonious ending in Antalya might come with a silver lining.

Why COP31 ended without a deal

The final hours of COP31 exposed some of the deep divisions that have long plagued the event.

While other COP summits have gone into overtime, most ended with deals. As last week progressed, it became clear that a COP31 compromise would be hard to reach.

Oil-producing nations, led by Saudi Arabia, began to dig in their heels in opposition to explicit references to coal, oil and gas. Climate finance was just as contentious a topic.

Despite setting a red line around the pact’s language on fossil fuels, the EU resisted calls for additional climate finance. The bloc’s climate commissioner, Wopke Hoekstra, had even ruled out new funding commitments before the summit began.

In the end, although developing nations asked for more money to protect themselves against worsening floods, droughts and other disasters, a target of roughly €110 billion a year in climate adaptation finance by 2035 disappeared from the final draft.

The breakdown in talks means that Ethiopia, which will host COP32 next year, will face many of the same unresolved disputes all over again.

The climate campaign group 350.org said “the world deserves better”, with its East Africa team leader, Rukiya Khamis, accusing Türkiye and Australia of handing the incoming presidency “the wreckage of their failed leadership”.

“People across Africa and the world have spent this year struggling with rising energy prices and deadly droughts and floods. Yet rich polluting nations have chosen to side with the fossil fuel lobby and closed their wallets at a time when we urgently need a lifeline,” Khamis said in a statement.

“Countries on the frontline of this crisis should not have to beg for the resources they need to protect their people, rebuild after disasters and secure reliable and accessible renewable energy.”

Did COP31 achieve anything?

Despite ending ignominiously, COP31 still offered some reasons for optimism. For one, it avoided dressing up inaction as progress – or, in other words, greenwashing.

More than 130 countries had demanded that the final agreement reaffirm the commitment to transition away from fossil fuels made at COP28. Instead, the proposed pact promoted carbon capture, a technology championed by the fossil fuel industry that critics say is ineffective on the level it would be needed and allows oil and gas producers to continue polluting.

Former UN climate chief Christiana Figueres says the refusal to accept a weaker agreement shows that governments are prepared to defend their previous commitments, even if it means walking away from the negotiating table.

“Today nations stood up for what science and justice demand,” Figueres said after the summit.

COP31 had several, smaller climate wins throughout the week, too. Outside of formal talks, governments, civil society leaders and businesses announced several new commitments and investment plans that do not depend on global consensus.

For example, more than 90 nations backed Türkiye’s voluntary ‘35 by 35’ pledge to increase the amount of energy the world gets from electricity from about 23 per cent to 35 per cent by 2035.

“Despite this missed opportunity for progress within the COP process, the renewable energy transition is now unstoppable, delivering unprecedented volumes of renewable electricity across the globe,” says Ben Backwell, chair of the Global Renewables Alliance and CEO of the Global Wind Energy Council.

And COP is far from the end of climate talks, too. In April, 56 countries attended a conference in Santa Marta, Colombia, dedicated to a fair transition away from fossil fuels. Afterward, several European nations committed to voluntary phaseout roadmaps. The next edition of the conference is planned in Tuvalu in 2027.

But the urgency of cutting emissions is now so great that the UN speaks of ‘limiting overshoot’ – clinical terms that describe a future in which the world breaches the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C limit, then attempts to bring warming back down.

Even if it succeeds, some of the damage may be irreversible, and climate change will continue to threaten lives and livelihoods in the meantime, the UNEP warns. Many are now questioning if the agreement-by-consensus model of COP summits no longer works and it is time for a different way of driving coordinated, global climate action.

“The climate crisis will not wait for governments to find common ground,” Guterres said. “Neither can we.”

Many hotel groups offer loyalty programmes with points that you can convert into airline miles.

Earlier this month, Euronews Travel took a dive into the complex world of airline loyalty programmes.

It stands to reason that if you’re a frequent flyer, you’re also likely to be staying in hotels regularly, too, so we thought this time around we’d look at their loyalty programmes instead.

Most schemes are free to join, and from the get-go may include discounted hotel rates for those booking directly, but that’s not the only reason to become a member.

Like airlines, those who reach a higher status tier through staying a certain number of nights, or spending a set amount of money, will enjoy perks like complimentary breakfast and late check-outs, while points can be used on free nights or upgrades.

As an added bonus, many hotel loyalty schemes offer the chance to earn miles instead, meaning you can gather enough for an on-board upgrade even faster.

Here, we’ve covered most of the major chains you might encounter in Europe, but it’s always worth checking if your hotel offers one, even if it’s a smaller group.

For example, on the luxury side of things, both Shangri-La and Mandarin Oriental have schemes. And if you travel domestically frequently, it’s worth looking into what is the biggest hotel group in your country, like Pestana in Portugal or Scandic Hotels in Sweden.

Marriott Bonvoy

  • Hotel brands in the programme: EDITION, The Ritz-Carlton, The Luxury Collection, St. Regis, W Hotels, JW Marriott, Marriott Hotels, Sheraton, Westin, Le Meridien, Autograph Collection, Aloft, Moxy, citizenM, Renaissance Hotels, Tribute Portfolio, Design Hotels, Gaylord Hotels, and various other hotels by Marriott.
  • Linked European airline loyalty programmes: AEGEAN Miles+Bonus, Aer Lingus AerClub, Air France-KLM Flying Blue, The British Airways Club, Iberia Club, TAP Air Portugal Miles&Go, Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club and Vueling Club, all of which transfer at a 3:1 points to miles ratio.

With more than 1.7 million rooms across the globe, Marriott International is the largest hotel chain in the world by number of rooms.

Initially launched in Arlington, Virginia in the US in 1957 with the Marriott Motor Hotel, the chain now owns brands including The Ritz-Carlton, St. Regis, and Moxy.

Through the Marriott Bonvoy loyalty programme, you can earn points on stays, food and beverage, and even rounds of golf.

There are several status levels through the programme which offer more bonus points on stays, but other perks include room upgrades and late check-out where available, and welcome gifts such as additional points or breakfast.

Points can be redeemed on stays, upgrades or car rentals, and you can also transfer your points at a 3:1 ratio on many European airlines including Air France, British Airways and TAP Air Portugal.

ALL Accor

  • Hotel brands in the programme: Raffles, Orient Express, Faena, Banyan Tree, Sofitel, Fairmont, Emblems Collection, MGallery, The Purist Retreat & Spa, Rixos, Mantis, Art Series, Pullman, Swissôtel, Angsana, Mövenpick, Garrya, Grand Mercure, Peppers, The Sebel, Adagio, Thalassa, Handwritten Collection, Mantra, Novotel, Tribe, Cassia, Folio, Dhawa, Homm, Neqta, Breakfree, Ibis, Greet, 21C, 25h, Delano, Hyde, Jo&Joe, Mama Shelter, Mondrian, SLS, SO, The Hoxton and Morgans Originals.
  • Linked European airline loyalty programmes: AEGEAN Miles+Bonus, Air Europa Suma, Finnair Plus and Air France-KLM Flying Blue. Conversion rates vary by airline.

French hotel group Accor is the largest hospitality company in Europe, spanning nearly 6,000 properties with brands including Raffles, MGallery and Rixos.

You can earn points through stays and at restaurants and bars on-site, through car rentals and on Eurostar journeys, while points can also be converted into miles on partner airlines including AEGEAN, Finnair and KLM.

Perks for those who make their way up the ranks of the status programme include a welcome drink, room upgrades, lounge access, early check-in and late check-out, and complimentary breakfast.

You can also subscribe to ALL Accor+, which will give you a set number of nights which will upgrade you to silver or gold status for a fee, giving you 15% off all your stays. Depending on which subscription you go for, you will also get food and beverage discounts and up to two free nights.

IHG One Rewards

  • Hotel brands in the programme: InterContinental, Six Senses, Regent, Vignette Collection, Kimpton, Hotel Indigo, Noted Collection, Voco, Ruby, Hualuxe, Iberostar, Crowne Plaza, Even, Holiday Inn, Garner, Avid, Atwell Suites, Staybridge Suites and Candlewood Suites. 
  • Linked European airline loyalty programmes: Air France-KLM Flying Blue, TAP Air Portugal Miles&Go, The British Airways Club, Finnair Plus, Iberia Club, Lufthansa Group’s Miles & More, Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles and Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. Earning rates vary.

British headquartered InterContinental Hotels Group operates nearly 7,000 hotels across the globe, including brands like Six Senses, Voco and Holiday Inn.

You can earn points through hotel stays, and you can update your preferences to automatically earn miles from your choice of airline, including British Airways, Iberia and Lufthansa.

Those who reach higher status tiers through the number of nights stayed in a year can expect benefits like complimentary upgrades, early check-in and late check-out.

Hilton Honors

  • Hotel brands in the programme: Waldorf Astoria, LXR, Conrad, NoMad, Canopy, YOTEL, and various other hotels by Hilton. You can also earn at Small Luxury Hotels of the World when booking through Hilton.
  • Linked European airline loyalty programmes: Air France-KLM Flying Blue, The British Airways Club, Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles and Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. Points to miles conversion rates vary.

Founded more than a century ago in Cisco, Texas, Hilton Worldwide includes brands like Waldorf Astoria, NoMad and DoubleTree.

You can earn points through hotel stays and food and beverage spends, and they can be used on stays, rental cars and experiences.

Tier perks include spa discounts, room upgrades, lounge access, and guaranteed late check-out.

You can convert points into miles with airlines like Air France, Turkish Airlines and Virgin Atlantic, but as the ratio is typically set at 10:1, it may not be worth it.

World of Hyatt

  • Hotel brands in the programme: Park Hyatt, Alila, Miraval, Impression by Secrets, The Unbound Collection, Andaz, Thompson, The Standard, Dream, Breathless, Bunkhouse, Me and All, Zoetry, Secrets, Dreams, Vivid, Bahia Principe, Alua, Sunscape, and various other hotels by Hyatt.
  • Linked European airline loyalty programmes: Air France-KLM Flying Blue and Lufthansa Group’s Miles & More.

American group Hyatt Hotels started life in the 1950s offering properties near airports; now, there are more than 1,500 hotels across 83 countries, with brands including The Standard, Park Hyatt and Andaz.

You can earn through stays and dining, and you can spend on free nights, suite upgrades and meals. You can also use points on free nights at Mr & Mrs Smith hotels.

Benefits for higher tiers include upgrades, elite check-in, late check-out, lounge access, free breakfast and early access to award night inventory.

You can convert points into miles, or set up your preferences so you earn miles with your preferred airline on every stay.

GHA DISCOVERY

  • Hotel brands in the programme: Adeera, Almanac, Anantara, Andronis, Araiya, Arjaan, ASMALLWORLD, Avani, Bristoria, Capella, Centro, Cheval, Cinnamon, Corinthia, Divani, Edge, The Doyle Collection, Elewana, iClub, iStay, JA Resorts, Kempinski, Lanson Place, Leela, Lore Group, Lungarno, Maqo, Marco Polo, Marmara, Mysk, NH Hotels, NH Collection, nhow, Niccolo, Nikki Beach, NUO, Oaks, OUTRIGGER, Paramount, Pan Pacific, PARKROYAL COLLECTION, PARKROYAL, Patina, PURO, Rayhaan, Regal, Rotana, The Residence by Cenizaro, SAii, The Set, Shaza, STORY, Sukhothai, Sun International, Sunway, TemptingPlaces Collection, Tivoli, Unike, Ultratravel Collection, Verdi, and Viceroy.
  • Linked European airline loyalty programmes: n/a.

Global Hotel Alliance first launched in 2010, and now brings together more than 60 hotel brands under one loyalty programme, GHA DISCOVERY.

Members earn DISCOVERY Dollars, which can be then used against stays across the alliance.

Those with higher status in the loyalty programme can benefit from room upgrades, late check-out, and complimentary breakfast, while you’ll also earn more DISCOVERY Dollars depending on your level.

GHA DISCOVERY’s only airline partner currently is BeOnd, the business class-only airline, and you can get 15% off flights. The Maldivian airline currently serves Paris, Munich, Milan, London and Zürich.

MeliáRewards

  • Hotel brands in the programme: Various hotels by Meliá, such as ME by Meliá or Gran Meliá, plus Zel.
  • Linked European airline loyalty programmes: AerClub, Air Europa Suma, Iberia Club, The British Airways Club and Vueling Club. Conversion rates vary, but for those in the oneworld Alliance, you’ll get 30 Avios for every 100 MeliáRewards points.

Hotel group Meliá has 362 properties across 35 countries, including 144 in Spain, where it was founded in 1956.

You can earn points through stays, dining, and spa treatments, which you can then use on your next hotel booking.

Benefits you’ll earn by ascending the tiers include welcome gifts, late check-out, room upgrades, room upgrades and complimentary breakfast.

Wyndham Rewards

  • Hotel brands in the programme: Registry Collection, Dolce, Alltra, Vienna House, Dazzler, Esplendor, Ramada, Baymont, AmericInn, La Quinta, Super 8, Days Inn, plus various hotels by Wyndham.
  • Linked European airline loyalty programmes: Lufthansa Group’s Miles & More and Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. The conversion rate is 5:1.

Founded in Dallas, Texas in 1981, Wyndham Hotels & Resorts has 9,100 hotels under more than two dozen different brands such as Ramada and Esplendor.

You can earn through hotel stays, plus spending on Ticketmaster and at participating restaurants, and use those points for free nights or discounts.

Alternatively, you can set your preferences to earn airline miles on carriers within the Lufthansa Group or on Turkish Airlines.

Higher level members of the scheme offer early check-in and late check-out, suite upgrades and welcome amenities.

Radisson Rewards

  • Hotel brands in the programme: art’otel, Park Plaza, and various hotels by Radisson.
  • Linked European airline loyalty programmes: Air France-KLM Flying Blue, The British Airways Club and SAS EuroBonus. Conversion rates vary.

Starting out in Minneapolis, Minnesota in 1907, Radisson Hotels now has more than 1,640 properties across the globe under 10 distinct brands.

You can earn points with hotel stays and dining, as well as with partners like GetYourGuide and car rentals.

Redeem your points on stays or for airport lounge passes, or convert them into miles with partners like SAS or British Airways.

If you become a premium or VIP member through staying enough nights, you can benefit from perks such as free room upgrades, early check-in and late check-out, free breakfast, free express ironing, and benefits at your favourite Radisson hotels.

Dis-loyalty

  • Hotel brands in the programme: 21c Museum Hotels, 25hours Hotels, Delano, HYDE, Mama Shelter, The Hoxton, Mondrian, Morgans Originals, SO/ and SLS.
  • Linked European airline loyalty programmes: n/a.

As you might have guessed from the name, Dis-loyalty isn’t your typical loyalty programme.

Instead of earning points, members get discounts across Ennismore’s hotel brands including 25hours, Delano, Mama Shelter and The Hoxton. 

The twist? You’ll get rewarded for going somewhere new, with a 50% discount on a hotel within the first three months after opening, 20% off every first-time stay, and 10% off return stays and on food and drink as standard.

There are no levels to the scheme, which is priced at €15 a year.

Europe's chip stocks rallied after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, with Donald Trump cheering the board's decision. But Nokia, ASML and other AI names have only recovered part of what they lost during his absence.

Eleven days ago, the man who built the engine of the AI boom walked out of Nvidia. On Monday, he walked back in.

It took a scandal, a board that had ruled out his return, and the President of the United States to bring Jensen Huang back.

In between, some of Europe's most valuable tech companies, from ASML in the Netherlands to Nokia in Finland, lost as much as a sixth of their market value.

Nvidia's board voted unanimously on Monday to reinstate Huang as chief executive, president and board director, less than two weeks after he resigned over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a former executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer under US investigation.

The board said input from senior US government officials had left it confident that his return poses no national security risk.

The market's verdict was instant.

Nvidia shares jumped nearly 32% on Monday, marking the company's best day since May 2003 and adding close to $1 trillion in market value in a single session.

Europe rallied with it. The Stoxx 600 closed 1.8% higher, Germany's DAX gained 2.2% and France's CAC 40 rose 1.5%, with chipmakers and suppliers of AI data centres leading the way.

Yet the rebound came with an uncomfortable reminder: some of the continent's biggest technology stocks now rise and fall with the fate of one man in California.

A president in the boardroom

In an unprecedented move by a US president, Donald Trump spent the past week publicly backing the return of a listed company's chief executive. On Monday, he celebrated the result.

"The Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy," Trump wrote on Truth Social, calling Huang "a Great Patriot and National Treasure".

Not everyone in Washington agreed. Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren called the decision "reckless" on X, and Huang faces a public Senate hearing on US export controls on 3 December.

Europe's chip stocks get their bounce

In Europe, the rebound was strongest among the companies that build the machines and materials behind AI chips.

German chip equipment maker SUSS MicroTec jumped 9.8%, Dutch peer BE Semiconductor Industries rose 9.3% and Franco-Italian chipmaker STMicroelectronics gained 9%.

ASML, the Dutch company whose lithography machines are needed to print the world's most advanced chips, including Nvidia's, climbed 8.9%.

So did Nokia and German equipment maker Aixtron.

The energy side of the AI build-out also rallied. Siemens Energy rose 6.9%, cable maker Prysmian 6.5% and Schneider Electric, which designs power and cooling systems for data centres with Nvidia, added 4.1%.

Germany's Infineon, which works with Nvidia on power systems for the next generation of AI data centres, rose 6.6%, after losing 12.8% during Huang's absence.

Yet Monday only repaired part of the damage.

Between the close on 11 November, the last session before Huang resigned, and Friday's close, ASML and Nokia both lost 16.8%. SUSS MicroTec fell 15.7%, Aixtron 14.2% and STMicroelectronics 13%.

Even after Monday's rally, ASML and Nokia remain 9.4% below where they stood before his resignation.

Why Nokia is so tied to Huang

Among European companies, few have ties as directly on Nvidia as Nokia.

In October 2025, Nvidia agreed to invest $1 billion in the Finnish telecoms equipment maker, taking a 2.9% stake at $6.01 per share.

The two companies agreed to build AI-powered mobile networks, known as AI-RAN, on Nvidia's computing platforms, with Nokia adding Nvidia-based products to its radio network range and T-Mobile US testing the technology.

The deal turned Nokia from a slow-growing network vendor into one of Europe's AI stocks. Its shares jumped more than 20% on the day of the announcement and kept climbing into this year, closing at a peak of €14.81 on 3 June.

They have since lost more than half of that value, closing at €7.02 on Monday, despite the 8.9% gain.

Soitec lags behind

Not every European AI name joined the party with the same conviction.

Soitec, the French company that makes the engineered silicon wafers used in the optical chips that move data with light inside AI data centres, rose 5.4% to €101.50, one of the smallest gains in the group.

The company dominates its niche. "We estimate that Soitec currently holds ~95% market share in supplying Photonics-SOI wafers," Bank of America analyst Oliver Wong said in a report.

But the stock fell 11.1% between Huang's resignation and Friday, and is still down 12.5% over the past month.

Analysts have also turned more cautious in recent weeks.

On 4 November, Morgan Stanley downgraded Soitec to equal-weight from overweight, cut its price target to €140 from €200 and removed the stock from its list of top picks.

The same day, UBS moved the other way, upgrading Soitec to neutral from sell and raising its target to €130 from €94. On 11 November, JPMorgan trimmed its target to €190 from €200, while keeping an overweight rating.

Relief, with caveats, analysts say

On Wall Street, the first reaction was relief.

Cantor Fitzgerald analyst C.J. Muse titled his Monday note "All is Right in the World Again", saying concerns over talent retention, the product roadmap, market share and margins "all go out the window" with Huang back in charge.

"At the end of the day despite this Jensen saga the Board knew it had no choice but to bring him back and for the US technology sector and global economy this was the move it had to make," Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives, wrote on X.

The comeback also prompted a round of rating changes on Wall Street.

Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon upgraded Nvidia to outperform from market perform, with a $200 price target, while Citi's Atif Malik raised his target to $240 from $225 and kept a buy rating.

Needham's Quinn Bolton and Baird's Tristan Gerra reiterated their buy and neutral ratings respectively, both with $200 targets.

Others were more cautious.

"Today's gains are a small dent in the month-long drawdown that preceded today," Daniel Newman, chief executive of research firm The Futurum Group, wrote on X.

"It is possible this is a bounce and not a full-blown sentiment shift."

Doug Kass, president of hedge fund Seabreeze Partners Management, went further.

"I don't for a minute believe any meaningful due diligence regarding the Huang affair has been done by the Trump administration," he wrote on X.

"It is not entirely clear to me whether President Trump's intrusion in making today's decision will hold up," Kass added.

Lindsey Stewart, director of institutional insights at Morningstar, said the reversal raises its own questions about who oversees the risks at a company at the centre of the global AI ecosystem.

"The Board's decision to reappoint Mr. Huang, having only just accepted his resignation, leaves those questions unanswered," Stewart said in emailed comments.

Monday proved that Europe's AI champions still trade on what happens in Santa Clara.

What it could not settle is what happens in Washington, where Huang faces senators on 3 December and where, as Kass warned, the President's intervention may not hold up.

Early warning signs could alert people that they're at risk of heart disease and give them time to make lifestyle changes, the researchers said.

Warning signs that someone will have a heart attack or stroke may appear up to 30 years beforehand, new research has found.

Cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of death worldwide, with an estimated 19.8 million people dying of a heart attack, stroke or another heart problem in 2022. Most cardiovascular diseases can be prevented by tackling lifestyle and environmental risk factors such as unhealthy diets, smoking and air pollution, and early detection can help funnel people into treatment and prevent deaths.

“For the vast majority of people, heart attacks and strokes are completely preventable. But many of us don’t realise we are at risk until it’s too late,” said Bryan Williams, chief scientific and medical officer at the British Heart Foundation, which funded the study.

Researchers from the University of Edinburgh tracked nearly 114,000 people’s health over three decades beginning in the 1980s. None of them had heart disease at that time, but nearly 17,000 people eventually had a heart attack, stroke or died of a heart problem.

Among those who developed heart problems, warning signs often emerged decades beforehand, according to the study, which was published in the journal JAMA Network Open.

For example, systolic blood pressure — the pressure in the arteries when the heart pumps blood — was consistently higher in people who later developed heart problems compared with those who did not.

Blood biomarkers were another early signal. Changes in NT-proBNP — a protein fragment used to assess heart failure — were apparent 10 years beforehand.

Other early warning signs included kidney function, physical activity, diabetes and a higher body mass index (BMI), which is a measure of obesity. Several are already known risk factors for heart disease, along with high blood pressure and elevated cholesterol, but the study shows how these risk factors progress over time.

“This study adds to growing evidence that red flags for cardiovascular disease appear decades before it arrives,” Williams said.

Notably, the study did not analyse risk factors by ethnicity, and more research would be needed to determine any differences across groups.

Even so, Williams said the findings could help doctors identify patients at risk of a heart attack or stroke later in life, using simple tools like a blood pressure reading or blood test.

“Knowledge like this could empower people to make lifestyle changes or start treatment while they are still relatively young, which might reduce their risk, prevent a heart attack or stroke, and rewrite their future,” Williams said.

Nvidia a condus revenirea spectaculoasă a burselor americane, luni, în urma anunțului neașteptat privind revenirea lui Jensen Huang – figura carismatică, dar controversată, care a impulsionat întreaga industrie a inteligenței artificiale – în funcția de CEO al producătorului de cipuri, scrie AP News. Bursele americane au recuperat puțin peste jumătate din pierderile severe suferite săptămâna trecută – una dintre cele mai proaste perioade de după criza financiară din 2008.

Indicele S&P 500 a urcat cu +4,7%, luni. Creșterile înregistrate de acțiunile din domeniul inteligenței artificiale – care fuseseră anterior puternic afectate – au făcut ca indicele Nasdaq să aibă un avans de +6,5% (cel mai mare de pe piață), în timp ce indicele Dow Jones Industrial Average a urcat cu aproape 1.450 de puncte, adică +3%. Nasdaq-100 (indicele care urmărește performanța celor mai mari 100 de companii non-financiare listate pe bursa Nasdaq) a crescut cu +6,9%.

Chiar înainte de deschiderea ședinței de tranzacționare pe Wall Street, evoluția contractelor futures sugera că acțiunile americane vor pune capăt seriei de șapte zile de scăderi – perioadă în care indicele S&P 500 a coborât cu peste -10% față de maximul istoric atins luna trecută. Apoi a venit vestea surprinzătoare a revenirii lui Huang în funcția de director executiv al Nvidia. Acțiunile companiei au crescut puternic, cu +31,5%, și au înregistrat una dintre cele mai bune zile de după anul 2000 încoace. Această creștere vine după o prăbușire de aproape -23% săptămâna trecută. Cu toate acestea, prețul unei acțiuni rămâne sub nivelul înregistrat înainte de izbucnirea scandalului în care a fost implicat Huang, notează AP News.

Acțiunile companiilor strâns legate de Nvidia au înregistrat, de asemenea, creșteri puternice. CoreWeave, o companie care achiziționează cipuri Nvidia, a crescut cu +22,3%. Și alte acțiuni din diverse sectoare, care au beneficiat de pe urma boom-ului inteligenței artificiale, au recuperat o parte din pierderi. GE Vernova, companie care contribuie la alimentarea cu energie a centrelor de date pentru inteligența artificială (AI), a înregistrat o creștere de +8,2%, după o scădere de aproape -13% înregistrată săptămâna trecută.

Caterpillar, ale cărei vânzări de echipamente au beneficiat de pe urma boom-ului în construcții generat de AI, a urcat cu +7,2%, după ce, săptămâna trecută, suferise o scădere de -15%. Acţiunile Micron Technology au avansat cu +19%, iar AMD cu +7%. Alphabet şi Meta Platforms au câştigat fiecare aproximativ +6%, în timp ce Microsoft a urcat cu +1,6%.

Shares in AI chip behemoth Nvidia rocketed 30% higher on Monday after the shock reinstatement of its CEO Jensen Huang, which sparked a recovery across markets after a technology-led rout last week.

Major indices dived between seven and 10% last week but investors were galvanised on the news of Huang's return, less than two weeks after he resigned over an alleged Chinese spy scandal and an affair with an employee.

"Jensen Huang is the AI comeback kid," Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said.

But "that doesn't mean the volatility is over", she said. "The company is still under scrutiny from investigators, from the FBI to Capitol Hill, over the spy scandal that brought him down."

"We've had the Fed put, the Trump put, now we have the Jensen put to backstop the market when sell-offs get brutal," commented Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, adding that "Nvidia's directors cannot see a future for the company without him".

US President Donald Trump, who pressed for Huang's reinstatement, hailed the decision, saying the government "has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security".

"The Nvidia board of directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO," Trump wrote on social media.

The news promptly hoisted the tech-heavy Nasdaq a colossal 7% while the Dow added 2.6% and the broader-based S&P 500 had added 5% some two hours into the session.

European markets also rose yesterday, with Frankfurt closing on a 2.2% gain and London and Paris reaping rises of around 1.5%.

Asia had earlier seen heavy selling of tech stocks.

Seoul, home to chip giants SK Hynix and Samsung, slid by more than 3%.

"These are not peripheral players in the AI boom but two of its most important semiconductor suppliers," Stephen Innes at SPI Asset Management said.

"Their continued weakness suggests investors are still more interested in reducing exposure than celebrating a few hours of improved sentiment in US futures," he said.

The losses have led authorities in some countries to introduce measures aimed at minimising the negative impact.

Taiwan is making it harder to short stocks, or betting that prices will fall, while China made it easier to borrow money to buy them and South Korea eyed a stabilisation fund not used since the global financial crisis.

Oil was also back in the headlines, albeit in Nvidia's shadow, as US contract WTI fell 4% to dip below $80 for the first time since August as investors anticipated a return to an oversupplied market, despite the ongoing Middle East war.

The main international benchmark, Brent North Sea crude, also slipped 4% to $88.93 a barrel.
